title: Durga, Kali, Lakshmi, Saraswati, Parvati as characters
hook: a young ascetic visits Parvati in the forest and mocks the god she loves, and she won't stay to listen
carry: Durga, Kali, Lakshmi, Saraswati, Parvati as characters

segments.voice: Yesterday closed a week of Durga, Kali, Lakshmi and Saraswati, ending with Saraswati as the speech in a giant's mouth. Today, the last of the five.

A princess has left her father's palace in the Himalayas for the forest. She tried to win the great ascetic Shiva the ordinary way: beauty, flowers, the god of love himself taking aim at Shiva. It went badly. Shiva opened his third eye, burned the god of love to ash, and walked away. So the princess changes her plan. If Shiva lives by austerity, she will out-austere him. In Kalidasa's poem, The Birth of Kumara, that's where we find her: alone in the forest, taking up the life of an ascetic. Today, Parvati.
screen: `A PRINCESS LEAVES THE PALACE.` → `LOVE IS BURNED TO ASH.` → `SHE CHANGES HER PLAN.`

segments.voice: Kalidasa describes her austerity season by season: standing among fires in the summer heat, in cold water through winter nights, living on less and less, until she gives up eating even fallen leaves. That, the poem says, is why those who know the old stories call her Aparna, the one without even a leaf. One day a visitor comes: a young ascetic with matted hair, polite, admiring. He asks why someone so lovely is doing all this. When he learns it's for Shiva, he starts, very gently, to make fun of her choice. Shiva? Who wears snakes and ash, rides an old bull, haunts cremation grounds? Nobody even knows his family. A princess like you, with him? Parvati doesn't laugh along, and she doesn't crumble. She defends Shiva point by point, then does something sharper. She tells her companion to stop him, because whoever speaks badly of a great soul does wrong, and so does whoever stays and listens. And she turns to walk away. Then the young ascetic drops the disguise. He was Shiva all along, testing her. In the poem he says that from now on he's hers, won by her austerity. So here is Parvati as a character. Not a girl waiting to be chosen. She chooses, outlasts the god of austerity at his own practice, and won't stand still while he's insulted to her face, even when it's him doing the insulting.
screen: `AUSTERITY, SEASON BY SEASON.` · `APARNA: NOT EVEN A LEAF.` · `A VISITOR MOCKS HER CHOICE.` · `SHE TURNS TO WALK AWAY.` · then, large: `IT WAS SHIVA ALL ALONG.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone or something you're devoted to that others don't quite understand, a person, a calling, a practice, and hear the gentle mocking voice for a moment: really, that? Notice what in you answers, not with anger, just steady, and let that steadiness sit in the spine and the breath. If you pray, bring that devotion before Parvati or God; if you don't, just stay steady.
Durga. The name over these five; and some Hindus hear Parvati and Durga as one Goddess in two moods: the patient one in the forest, the warrior on the lion. Today's word.

howItsDone: Parvati's austerity to win Shiva is remembered in festivals such as Hartalika Teej, when some Hindu women fast and pray in her honor, and her story is told in the Puranas and in Kalidasa's poem.

notes: Kumarasambhava canto 5 paraphrased (no PD translation on the validator list). Confirm: the five-fires summer austerity and winter water, giving up fallen leaves (5.28, Aparna), the brahmacharin's mockery (snakes, ash, bull, cremation ground, unknown lineage), her rebuke that the listener also incurs sin, her turning to leave, and Shiva's words that he is now her servant 'bought by austerity'. The title 'The Birth of Kumara' is a translation of the poem's name.
The burning of Kama is in canto 3; Shiva Purana tells the same arc. Day 679 described Parvati as Brahmacharini briefly; this day tells the poem's scene.
'Some Hindus hear Parvati and Durga as one Goddess in two moods' is attributed; confirm.
